citations.review_note: Verified 2026-09-05 against PMID 24413700, Crossref 10.1038/nn.3616 and the full text at PMC4442489. citations.authors: Adkin AL, Frank JS, Carpenter MG, Peysar GW
citations.title: Postural control is scaled to level of postural threat
citations.review_note: Verified 2026-09-05 against PMID 10998604: authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and year are all correct. What the paper found: 62 healthy young adults (20.3 +/- 1.3 y) stood quietly on a force plate at 40, 100 and 160 cm above ground; centre-of-pressure amplitude fell and its frequency rose linearly as postural threat increased, i.e. the nervous system progressively tightened postural control under threat. It recorded centre-of-pressure kinematics only. Corrected 2026-09-05: the record is sound, but the claim attached to it in handstand-walk prose ('postural threat alters muscle activation before the fall') is not this paper's finding, because no EMG was recorded here; that result belongs to carpenter_frank_2001. The 'Adkin & Frank 2002' companion cited alongside it in the same sentence has no entry in this library and was not located.
citations.id_note: Identifier, byline and bibliographic fields all correct. The defect was the claim attached to it in prose: this study measured centre-of-pressure only, contains no EMG, and was credited with a muscle-activation finding that belongs to Carpenter 2001. The paired 'Adkin & Frank 2002' has no record here.

citations.authors: Carpenter MG, Frank JS, Silcher CP, Peysar GW
citations.title: The influence of postural threat on the control of upright stance
citations.display_line: Carpenter et al. (2001), Exp Brain Res 138(2)
citations.review_note: Verified 2026-09-05 against PMID 11417462: authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and year are all correct. What the paper found: eight young healthy adults in quiet upright stance under three levels of postural threat (up to 81 cm elevation) adopted a stiffening strategy under high threat, with significant changes in kinematic, kinetic and EMG variables and an anterior-posterior stiffness constant 27.5% higher than at low threat. This is the correct source for the claim that postural threat changes muscle activation. Corrected 2026-09-05: the record is sound, but 'anxiety degrades balance strategy' overstates it two ways. The paper reports a different strategy (stiffening), not a demonstrated decrement, and anxiety was not the manipulated variable - elevation was. n = 8, quiet bipedal stance, no inversion and no hand support.
citations.id_note: Identifier and byline correct. The defect was interpretive: a change of postural strategy under threat was reported as a degradation of balance, and threat was read as anxiety.

citations.title: Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis
citations.review_note: Verified 2026-09-05 against PMID 17762369: authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and year all exact. Full text is closed (Unpaywall reports oa_status closed, no OA locations), so only the abstract was retrievable. What the paper found: 27 of 182 screened studies met inclusion; the optimal strategy is a 2-week taper (overall effect 0.59 +/- 0.33, p < 0.001) in which training volume is exponentially decreased by 41-60% (overall effect 0.72 +/- 0.36, p < 0.001) without modifying training intensity or frequency. Corrected 2026-09-05: it was described in rowing-2k-test-prep as the stronger single-source anchor for a ~3% performance uplift. The retrievable record reports standardised effect sizes, not percentages, and no 3% figure appears in it; the same 3% is attributed elsewhere in that programme to Mujika & Padilla 2000. The structural prescription this paper supports verbatim; the quantified promise it does not, and full text would be needed to close the question.
citations.id_note: Identifier and bibliographic fields correct. The defect is the number: a percentage uplift was credited to a meta-analysis that reports standardised effect sizes, with full text unavailable to check.

citations.display_line: Yiou et al. (2017), World J Orthop 8(11)
citations.review_note: Verified 2026-09-05 against PMID 29184756: authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and year all correct. What the paper is: a state-of-the-art review of balance control during bipedal gait initiation from quiet standing, covering anticipatory postural adjustments, stance-leg stiffness, foot placement, lateral ankle strategy, swing-foot strike pattern and vertical centre-of-mass braking, framed for aging, neurological and orthopedic conditions and aimed at rehabilitation targeting. Corrected 2026-09-05: it is cited in handstand-walk for initiating locomotion on the hands while inverted. The general point it does license - a postural shift precedes the first step rather than following it - is real; nothing in the paper addresses inversion, hand support, or a base of support at the hands. Note also that it entered the record as a replacement for an unlocatable citation (ferrari_2021), which is the situation in which a near-enough substitution is easiest to make.
citations.id_note: Identifier and byline correct. The defect is population and task: a review of able-bodied and frail bipedal gait initiation applied to handstand walking.

citations.review_note: Verified 2026-09-05 via Crossref 10.1016/j.jelekin.2016.11.004 and PMID 28011412: authors, title, journal, volume, pages and year all exact; DOI and link added, both previously absent. What the paper found: peak and average rectified EMG of the shoulder-arm-forearm complex in 19 strength-trained males across four conditions - supinated, pronated, neutral and rope pull-ups. Its conclusion is that activation is SIMILAR across hand orientations despite the differing grips, with the exception of middle trapezius in pronated versus neutral; the clear difference it does report is between concentric and eccentric phases, with brachioradialis, biceps brachii and pectoralis major significantly more active concentrically. citations.id_note: Record correct but unlinked and marked pending. The defect is claim-fit: false grip was never studied, and the paper concludes hand orientation largely does NOT differentiate activation, which is the reverse of what it was cited for.
